source.version: Journal version of record: Dirasat: Educational Sciences, Volume 53, No. 3, 2026, article 13368; received 28/9/2025, revised 11/12/2025, accepted 2/2/2026, published 25/2/2026 (p. 1). Body text is in Arabic; title and abstract also in English.
source.title_on_document: Effectiveness of a Training Program Based on Artificial Intelligence Tools in Developing Creative Problem-Solving Skills

supplement.holds: No supplementary material or online appendix is mentioned in the full document. The PDF ends with references; outcome statistics are in main-text Tables 4-7 (pp. 10-13).

paper_design_summary: The paper reports random assignment of three intact tenth-grade classes in one school to AI-tool training, classroom training, or no training, with 25 students per class (75 assigned). Both training arms used an Osborn-Parnes creative problem-solving program; the AI arm used ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot in a computer lab, while the active comparison used classroom strategies. Verbal Torrance test responses were scored for fluency, flexibility, and originality before, immediately after, and at follow-up; final analysis counts and AI availability during the tests are not explicitly reported.

studies.label: Three-class school trial: AI-tool training, classroom training, and control

assignment.what_was_assigned: Three intact classes were randomly assigned to AI-tool training, classroom training, or control, with one class in each condition. Individual students were not redistributed. This is class-level random assignment despite the authors also using the label quasi-experimental.
assignment.quote: The classes were randomly assigned to three groups:
assignment.locator: p. 1, English abstract, Methods; p. 5, study limitations; p. 6, study population and sample; p. 9, design diagram. Ordinary school activity periods: p. 10, procedures.

arms.name: AI-tool training (2EG)
arms.description: Osborn-Parnes creative problem-solving program in the computer lab with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot. The 20-session program includes opening/pre-test and closing/post-test sessions; tools are named for sessions 2-19 (pp. 7-9, Table 2).

arms.name: Classroom training (1EG)
arms.description: The same program using classroom instruction, brainstorming, problem-based and project-based learning, think-pair-share, flipped learning, and synectics, without AI (p. 7).

arms.name: Control (CG)
arms.description: No training program; the same pre-, post-, and follow-up tests were administered (p. 1, Methods; p. 9, design diagram).

participants.exclusions: The reported sample and assignment count is 75, with 25 students per class/arm. The abstract says tests were administered to all participants, but no separate final analysis count, exclusions statement, or arm-specific analysis denominator is printed. Table 5 reports error df = 72; no analyzed count is derived from those degrees of freedom. The separate 25-student psychometric pilot is explicitly outside the main sample (p. 6).
participants.who: Tenth-grade students in three intact mixed-gender classes at one Arab school in Haifa District, selected by convenience through the first author workplace; 41 male and 34 female students. The stated sampling frame comprised 3719 students across 38 Arab schools of Haifa District (p. 6).
participants.country: Not explicitly named as a country; the paper describes Arab schools in Haifa District inside the Green Line (p. 6).
participants.quote: The sample comprised 75 students distributed across three intact mixed-gender tenth-grade classes in a single school.
participants.locator: p. 1, English abstract, Methods; p. 6, study population and sample; pp. 10-11, Table 4 and p. 11, Table 5 (no analysis n).

ai_tool.how_used: Use during a structured, instructor-led creative problem-solving training program. ChatGPT supported interactive dialogue and idea generation, Gemini supported varied ideas, and Copilot supported novel solutions (p. 7, training strategies). Table 2 names a tool for each training session, but does not establish unrestricted chatbot use. Availability during the separately scored TTCT administrations is not stated (pp. 8-10).

task.description: Verbal Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, Form A, adapted to the Jordanian context by Al-Shanti (1983). The original seven subtests were reduced to six by omitting the sixth for low reliability. Fluency, flexibility, and originality were scored on test responses (p. 6). Training used general problems such as environmental pollution, water shortages, and space exploration (p. 10).
task.duration: Program: 20 sessions, three per week, 4 May-12 June 2025; training sessions last 45 minutes and the opening and closing sessions 60 minutes (p. 7; pp. 8-9, Table 2). Test duration is not separately stated. Post-test in the final session; follow-up on 4 September 2025 (p. 10). No delay in days is printed.

outcomes.name: TTCT fluency, post-test
outcomes.measure_detail: Verbal TTCT fluency score under the adopted test instructions. The separate 25-student pilot used manual response scoring and rescoring by two educational-psychology specialists; Table 1 reports test-retest reliability 0.80 and Holsti scoring agreement 0.75 (p. 6). The paper does not give the main-sample scorers credentials or the detailed count/rubric procedure, so the categorical measure field is null. The intended training-transfer question is after_ai, but the paper does not explicitly establish AI removal during testing; question and ai_available_when_produced therefore remain null.
outcomes.delay: Post-test in the closing session of the program ending 12 June 2025 (p. 9, Table 2; p. 10, procedures).

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is met: the paper explicitly reports random assignment of three intact classes to generative-AI creative problem-solving training, classroom training without AI, or no training (p. 1, Methods; pp. 5-7, limitations, sample and training program). Class-level assignment supports field_rct despite the authors quasi-experimental label. Criterion 2 and core eligibility remain unclear: the 75 students and 25 per arm are sample/allocation counts, and administration of tests to all participants does not explicitly state how many were analyzed (pp. 1 and 6). No final total or per-arm analyzed headcount or exclusions accounting is printed in Tables 4-7 (pp. 10-13); the error df = 72 in Table 5 is retained without deriving an analyzed count. Authors must confirm that at least 50 people were analyzed. Criterion 3 is met by fluency, flexibility and originality scored on participants verbal TTCT responses (p. 6, instrument and scoring; pp. 10-11, Table 4). Unspecified AI access during tests prevents assigning after_ai versus with_ai, but does not negate random assignment to AI training or scoring on output (pp. 8-10, Table 2 and procedures). Main-sample scorer details and uncertainty appropriate to one randomized class per arm affect measurement coding and pooling, not these eligibility criteria. The randomized study is not observational context.

one_line_finding: The AI-training class had higher TTCT originality means at post-test (29.32 vs 19.48 classroom training vs 8.51 control) and follow-up (28.16 vs 18.78 vs 7.74), with no printed pairwise between-group test (p. 11, Table 4).
open_questions: What total and per-arm numbers were included in the post-test, follow-up, and repeated-measures analyses, after any exclusions?
Was AI unavailable while participants produced TTCT responses at post-test and follow-up? Test timing and blank tool cells do not explicitly answer this.
Who scored the main-sample TTCT responses, were they blinded, and what counting/rating rules were used for each subscale? The named expert rescoring concerns the separate pilot.
Can class-level uncertainty be supported with one randomized class per arm? No cluster-adjusted analysis or pairwise between-arm precision is printed.
notes: The whole markdown, through p. 18 and the references, was read; no appendix is included. Retained numbers were checked against PDF text/tables. Class randomization supports field_rct despite the authors quasi-experimental label; one class per arm and no cluster-adjusted precision remain limitations. The AI arm also differs in setting (computer lab versus classroom, p. 7). All six outcome/time combinations are retained. Table 4 total rows pool groups, not creativity dimensions. No additional scored-output or diversity outcome was found. Null measure, question, and AI-availability values are intentional: the enums lack an unknown category. The intended question is after_ai, conditional on confirming AI removal during tests. The arm_means_sds_ns flag includes allocation counts only; analyzed counts are unknown. Table 5 labels effect sizes eta squared; no standardized pairwise effect was computed. Omnibus tests are not pairwise treatment effects. Table 5 prints time df = 1, interaction df = 2, and error df = 72 despite three time points; p. 10 describes Huynh-Feldt correction. The p. 10 Kolmogorov-Smirnov values are 0.083, 0.084, 0.078; Box test value is 1.342, all described as nonsignificant at 0.05. Table 7 spans pp. 12-13 and repeats within-group time comparisons despite its by-group heading. The AI fluency cell on p. 13 contains an extra asterisk. Table 6 prints post/follow-up difference 1.97; this was not recalculated from rounded means. Nonsignificance does not establish equivalence. Reconciliation groups repeated field differences and logs labelled shared-entry corrections. n_unresolved counts entries, including related count gaps. Equivalent wording, contrast order, empty synthesis templates, and equivalent page ranges are not differences. No supplement, preregistration, data/code release, cross-paper overlap, or company involvement is reported. Finalization: the full 74227-character markdown was read through the references, and the PDF has 18 pages. Source passages and retained numbers were checked against PDF text and table extraction. The assignment, outcome and people challenge files all contain empty problems lists, so challenge_resolution is empty and all challenge-resolution counters are zero; these counters do not count the existing open questions. The four final.open_items cover all four open_questions and all five unresolved reconciliation differences, grouping related count gaps. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged. Core eligibility remains unclear solely because the analyzed headcount is not explicit.

open_items.item: Final analyzed headcounts and exclusions by arm, measurement occasion and repeated-measures analysis (open_questions[0]; unresolved reconciliation fields studies.S1.arms[*].n_analyzed, studies.S1.outcomes[*].n_units, and studies.S1.participants.n_analyzed_and_eligibility.criterion_2). The source gives allocation counts and test administration, but no explicit final included headcounts (pp. 1 and 6; pp. 10-13, Tables 4-7). Authors participant accounting would settle criterion 2. The outcomes use participant units; their missing counts are the same analyzed-people gap, not additional samples.

AI access during post-test and follow-up (open_questions[1]; unresolved reconciliation field studies.S1.outcomes[*].ai_available_when_produced_and_question). Authors testing instructions must establish whether AI was available when the scored TTCT responses were produced. Blank tool cells and a discussion of absent later support do not settle the protocol (pp. 8-10, Table 2 and procedures; p. 14, discussion). This affects after_ai versus with_ai coding; criteria 1 and 3 are already supported.

Main-sample TTCT scorer qualifications, blinding and scoring/counting rules (open_questions[2]; unresolved reconciliation field studies.S1.outcomes[*].measure). Authors main-sample scoring protocol would settle the measure codes and blinding information. The two educational-psychology specialists are reported in the separate pilot reliability assessment (p. 6, reliability). These details do not overturn criterion 3: the outcomes are scores on produced TTCT responses (p. 6, instrument; pp. 10-11, Table 4).

Uncertainty appropriate to class assignment and pairwise between-arm comparisons (open_questions[3]). There is one randomized class per arm, and the printed analysis uses participant-level scores; no class-adjusted pairwise standard error or confidence interval is supplied (p. 6, sample; p. 9, statistical methods; pp. 11-13, Tables 5-7). Authors allocation and analysis details, with any defensible uncertainty estimate respecting class assignment, would settle whether an estimate can be pooled. This affects pooling and precision, not an eligibility criterion; additional participant-level data alone would not provide replicated classes.
